Vendor Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery Questionnaire Response - Prepared by: Ops Team, Fenwick Data Systems

Thank you for this questionnaire, we take business continuity very seriously here at Fenwick and wanted to give thorough answers rather than just checking boxes, so apologies in advance if some of these answers are longer than a typical form response, we figured more context is better than less for something this important.

Regarding our overall approach, we've been operating for about 11 years now and have been through a few real-world tests of our continuity planning, including a regional power outage in 2021 that affected our primary data center for about 6 hours, and a more recent incident in 2024 involving a fiber cut near our secondary facility that we'll get into more detail on below since it's actually pretty relevant to a few of your specific questions.

Our primary data center is in Ashburn, Virginia, and our secondary (failover) data center is in Phoenix, Arizona, chosen specifically for geographic diversity from a natural disaster perspective. Data replication between the two sites happens continuously with a target RPO (recovery point objective) of under 5 minutes, and our most recent measured actual RPO during a failover test in September was 3 minutes 40 seconds, so we're comfortably beating our own target.

Our target RTO (recovery time objective) is 4 hours for full service restoration. Here's where I want to be really transparent with you: during the 2024 fiber cut incident I mentioned above, our actual RTO was 6 hours and 15 minutes, not the 4 hours we target, because the automated failover script had a bug that required manual intervention partway through, which added roughly 2 hours to the process. We've since fixed that bug and re-tested successfully twice since then (most recently 3 months ago), both times achieving RTOs under 4 hours (3h 20m and 3h 45m respectively), but we wanted to be upfront that our target wasn't met during that one real incident, since I know some vendors gloss over that kind of thing and we'd rather you have the full picture.

We conduct full failover tests twice per year (typically April and October) and tabletop exercises quarterly. Backup retention is 90 days for daily backups and 7 years for monthly archival backups, stored encrypted (AES-256) in a third geographic location separate from both primary and secondary data centers.

On staffing continuity, we have documented succession plans for all key operational roles and cross-training such that no single person is the only one who knows how to execute any critical procedure - this was actually a gap we identified after a key engineer left unexpectedly in 2022, which is when we built out the current cross-training program.

One thing we do NOT currently have, and I want to flag this proactively rather than have you find it in an audit: we don't yet have a formal, contractually-committed continuity arrangement with a third-party disaster recovery vendor as a tertiary fallback beyond our own two data centers; it's on our roadmap for next year's budget cycle but isn't in place today. If that's a hard requirement on your end we'd want to discuss it directly rather than have you assume it's already covered.

Happy to answer any follow-up questions or hop on a call to walk through any of this in more detail, especially the 2024 incident since I imagine that's the part most likely to raise questions.

P.S. - one of our account reps mentioned you might also want details on physical security at the two data centers, so a quick note there too: both facilities are colocation space within larger third-party data center providers (not buildings we own ourselves), and physical access at both requires badge plus biometric verification, with visitor logs retained for 2 years. Neither of our two real-world incidents (the 2021 outage or the 2024 fiber cut) involved any physical security issue at either site; both were purely power and connectivity problems respectively, nothing related to unauthorized physical access. Let us know if you need the colocation providers' own SOC 2 reports as well, we can usually get those from them within a few business days on request.

Exclusions (do not count against uptime): scheduled maintenance windows (announced 48+ hours in advance, max 4 hours/month), and outages caused by Customer's own network/equipment. This month: total downtime logged was 6 hours out of 720 total hours, of which 3.5 hours was a scheduled maintenance window announced 72 hours in advance, and 1 hour was traced to a failure in Customer's own firewall configuration. Uptime percentage for SLA purposes therefore excludes those 4.5 hours, counting only the remaining 1.5 hours as SLA-applicable downtime.
